title: AP Statistics: Concepts and Formulas

sources.name: Original educational writing from general knowledge

description: For AP Statistics students reviewing data analysis, study design, probability, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests. Original concept and formula prompts with conditions stated.

cards.front: What is the difference between a population and a sample?
cards.back: A population is the full group of interest; a sample is the subset actually observed.

cards.front: What is a parameter?
cards.back: A numerical characteristic of a population, such as its mean or proportion.

cards.front: What is a statistic?
cards.back: A numerical summary computed from sample data.

cards.front: What is a categorical variable?
cards.back: A variable whose values identify groups or categories rather than numerical amounts.

cards.front: What is a quantitative variable?
cards.back: A variable whose numerical values represent measured or counted amounts for which arithmetic is meaningful.

cards.front: How do discrete and continuous quantitative variables differ?
cards.back: Discrete variables have countable possible values; continuous variables can vary across an interval of measurements.

cards.front: What does a distribution describe?
cards.back: The values a variable takes and how often or with what probability they occur.

cards.front: What features should a description of a quantitative distribution address?
cards.back: Shape, center, spread, and unusual features, interpreted in context.

cards.front: What is a right-skewed distribution?
cards.back: A distribution with a longer tail toward larger values.

cards.front: What is a left-skewed distribution?
cards.back: A distribution with a longer tail toward smaller values.

cards.front: How does a histogram differ from a bar chart?
cards.back: A histogram groups quantitative values into numerical intervals; a bar chart compares categorical counts or proportions.

cards.front: What does a cumulative relative-frequency graph show?
cards.back: The proportion of observations at or below each displayed value or boundary.

cards.front: What is the arithmetic mean of n observations?
cards.back: The sum of all observations divided by n.

cards.front: What is the median?
cards.back: The middle ordered value; for an even number of observations, the average of the two middle values.

cards.front: Which is generally more resistant to extreme values: mean or median?
cards.back: The median.

cards.front: What is the interquartile range?
cards.back: IQR = Q3 - Q1, describing the spread of the middle half of the data.

cards.front: What is the 1.5-IQR outlier rule?
cards.back: Flag values below Q1 - 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR as potential outliers.

cards.front: What five values form a five-number summary?
cards.back: Minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum.

cards.front: What does sample standard deviation measure?
cards.back: Typical spread around the sample mean, in the original units, using squared deviations and an n - 1 denominator.

cards.front: What is the formula for sample variance?
cards.back: s squared = sum of (x_i - x-bar) squared divided by n - 1.

cards.front: What happens to the mean and standard deviation when a constant c is added to every observation?
cards.back: The mean increases by c; the standard deviation is unchanged.

cards.front: What happens to the mean and standard deviation when every observation is multiplied by c?
cards.back: The mean is multiplied by c; the standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of c.

cards.front: What is a standardized z-score?
cards.back: z = (x - mean)/standard deviation, measuring how many standard deviations an observation lies from the mean.

cards.front: What does the kth percentile represent?
cards.back: A value with approximately k percent of the distribution at or below it, with precise sample conventions varying.

cards.front: What is the empirical rule for a roughly normal distribution?
cards.back: About 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of values lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean.

cards.front: What identifies a normal distribution?
cards.back: Its mean and standard deviation; its density is symmetric, bell-shaped, and has total area one.

cards.front: What is the standard normal distribution?
cards.back: A normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

cards.front: How is probability represented under a continuous density curve?
cards.back: As area under the curve over the relevant interval.

cards.front: What is the probability of exactly one specified value for a continuous random variable?
cards.back: Zero; probabilities apply to intervals even though individual outcomes occur.

cards.front: What does a scatterplot display?
cards.back: The relationship between two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals.

cards.front: What features should a scatterplot description include?
cards.back: Direction, form, strength, and unusual observations, in context.

cards.front: What does correlation r measure?
cards.back: The direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.

cards.front: What is the possible range of correlation r?
cards.back: -1 to 1, inclusive.

cards.front: Does correlation have measurement units?
cards.back: No. It is unitless.

cards.front: Does switching explanatory and response variables change correlation?
cards.back: No.

cards.front: Does correlation near zero rule out a strong relationship?
cards.back: No. A strong nonlinear relationship may have near-zero linear correlation.

cards.front: Why does correlation alone not establish causation?
cards.back: Confounding, reverse direction, or other mechanisms can produce association without the proposed cause.

cards.front: What is a least-squares regression line?
cards.back: The line minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals when predicting the response from the explanatory variable.

cards.front: How is a regression residual calculated?
cards.back: Observed response minus predicted response: y - y-hat.

cards.front: What is the least-squares slope in terms of r and sample standard deviations?
cards.back: b = r times s_y/s_x, when both standard deviations are positive.

cards.front: What point always lies on the least-squares regression line with an intercept?
cards.back: The point (x-bar, y-bar).

cards.front: How should a regression slope be interpreted?
cards.back: For a one-unit increase in x, the predicted y changes by the slope's amount, on average, within the model's scope.

cards.front: What does r squared mean in simple linear regression with an intercept?
cards.back: The proportion of observed variation in y explained by its linear regression on x.

cards.front: What is extrapolation?
cards.back: Using a model to predict beyond the observed range of explanatory values.

cards.front: What pattern supports a linear model in a residual plot?
cards.back: Random-looking scatter around zero with no clear curve and roughly constant vertical spread.

cards.front: What is an influential observation in regression?
cards.back: An observation whose removal substantially changes the fitted model.

cards.front: What is a high-leverage observation?
cards.back: An observation with an explanatory-variable value far from the other x values.

cards.front: What distinguishes an observational study from an experiment?
cards.back: An experiment imposes treatments; an observational study observes without assigning the exposure of interest.

cards.front: What is a confounding variable?
cards.back: A variable whose effect is mixed with the explanatory variable's effect, limiting separate causal interpretation.

cards.front: What is a simple random sample of size n?
cards.back: A sample selected so every possible subset of n population members has an equal chance of selection.

cards.front: What is a stratified random sample?
cards.back: Divide the population into relevant strata and randomly sample within each stratum.

cards.front: What is a cluster sample?
cards.back: Randomly select groups or clusters and observe all members of selected clusters in the basic design.

cards.front: What is a systematic sample?
cards.back: Choose a random starting point and then select every kth member of an ordered list.

cards.front: What is undercoverage?
cards.back: A sampling process leaves some population groups inadequately represented or excluded.

cards.front: What is nonresponse bias?
cards.back: Systematic error when nonrespondents differ in relevant ways from respondents.

cards.front: What is response bias?
cards.back: Systematic distortion in answers due to wording, interviewer effects, inaccurate reporting, or similar influences.

cards.front: Why are voluntary-response samples often biased?
cards.back: People self-select, and those with strong opinions or special motivation may be overrepresented.

cards.front: What is the purpose of random assignment?
cards.back: To create treatment groups comparable on average and support causal inference.

cards.front: What is the purpose of random sampling?
cards.back: To support generalization from a sample to the population sampled.

cards.front: What are the core principles of a well-designed comparative experiment?
cards.back: Comparison, random assignment, control of relevant conditions, and replication.

cards.front: What is replication in an experiment?
cards.back: Applying each treatment to enough independent experimental units to assess variability and treatment effects.

cards.front: What is a placebo?
cards.back: A treatment designed to resemble the active treatment without its specific active component.

cards.front: What does double-blind usually mean in an experiment?
cards.back: Neither the participants nor those evaluating outcomes know the treatment assignments, where feasible.

cards.front: What is blocking in an experiment?
cards.back: Grouping similar experimental units before randomizing treatments within each group.

cards.front: What is a matched-pairs design?
cards.back: An experiment comparing two treatments using paired similar units or the same unit under both conditions.

cards.front: What range must any probability fall within?
cards.back: From 0 to 1, inclusive.

cards.front: What is the complement rule?
cards.back: P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

cards.front: What is the general addition rule for two events?
cards.back: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).

cards.front: What does mutually exclusive mean?
cards.back: Two events cannot occur together, so their intersection has probability zero.

cards.front: Can mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities be independent?
cards.back: No. Occurrence of one rules out the other.

cards.front: What is conditional probability?
cards.back: P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B), provided P(B) is positive.

cards.front: What is the general multiplication rule?
cards.back: P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B given A).

cards.front: What does independence of two events mean?
cards.back: Knowing one occurred does not change the probability of the other; equivalently P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).

cards.front: How can an at-least-one probability often be computed efficiently?
cards.back: Subtract the probability of zero occurrences from 1.

cards.front: What is a discrete random variable's expected value?
cards.back: The sum of each possible value multiplied by its probability.

cards.front: What is a discrete random variable's variance?
cards.back: The sum of (value - mean) squared times its probability.

cards.front: What is the expected value of aX + b?
cards.back: aE(X) + b.

cards.front: What is the standard deviation of aX + b?
cards.back: The absolute value of a times the standard deviation of X.

cards.front: What is the mean of X + Y?
cards.back: E(X) + E(Y), whether or not X and Y are independent.

cards.front: For independent X and Y, what is the variance of X - Y?
cards.back: Var(X) + Var(Y); variances add even when the variables are subtracted.

cards.front: What conditions define a binomial setting?
cards.back: A fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes per trial, and the same success probability on every trial.

cards.front: What is the binomial probability formula?
cards.back: P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k), for k from 0 to n.

cards.front: What are a binomial variable's mean and standard deviation?
cards.back: Mean np; standard deviation square root of np(1 - p).

cards.front: What does a geometric random variable count in the usual AP convention?
cards.back: The number of independent trials through and including the first success, with constant success probability p.

cards.front: What is the geometric probability formula in the trials-until-success convention?
cards.back: P(X = k) = (1 - p)^(k - 1) p for k = 1, 2, and so on.

cards.front: What is the expected value of a geometric variable counting trials until first success?
What is a sampling distribution?
cards.back: The distribution of a statistic over repeated samples of the same size drawn by the same method.

cards.front: What makes an estimator unbiased?
cards.back: Its sampling-distribution mean equals the population parameter being estimated.

cards.front: How does increasing sample size generally affect sampling variability?
cards.back: It reduces variability; many standard errors scale as 1 divided by the square root of sample size.

cards.front: What is the mean of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion?
cards.back: The population proportion p, under the usual random-sampling conditions.

cards.front: What is the standard deviation of a sample proportion with independent trials?
cards.back: Square root of p(1 - p)/n.

cards.front: What is the usual 10% condition used for sampling without replacement?
cards.back: The sample size is at most 10% of the population, allowing approximate independence for standard-error formulas.

cards.front: What large-counts condition supports a normal approximation to a sample proportion?
cards.back: Expected successes np and failures n(1 - p) are each at least 10, using the appropriate p for the procedure.

cards.front: What are the mean and standard deviation of the sample mean for independent observations?
cards.back: Mean mu and standard deviation sigma divided by the square root of n.

cards.front: What does the central limit theorem say about sample means?
cards.back: With sufficiently large independent samples from a population with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal.

cards.front: If the population is normal, what is the shape of the sample mean's distribution?
cards.back: Normal for every sample size, assuming independent observations.

cards.front: What is the general form of a confidence interval?
cards.back: Point estimate plus or minus a critical value times its standard error.

cards.front: What does 95% confidence mean?
cards.back: In repeated sampling, about 95% of intervals made by the procedure would contain the fixed population parameter.

cards.front: Does a computed frequentist 95% interval give a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies in that particular interval?
cards.back: No. The confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the procedure.

cards.front: How does higher confidence affect interval width, all else equal?
cards.back: It increases the critical value and makes the interval wider.

cards.front: How does quadrupling sample size affect a standard error proportional to 1/sqrt(n)?
cards.back: It halves the standard error and approximately halves the margin of error at the same confidence level.

cards.front: What is the one-proportion z-interval formula?
cards.back: p-hat plus or minus z-star times square root of p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n, when conditions hold.

cards.front: When estimating sample size for a proportion with no prior estimate, which planning value is conservative?
cards.back: p = 0.5, which maximizes p(1 - p).

cards.front: What is the one-sample t-interval formula for a mean?
cards.back: x-bar plus or minus t-star times s/sqrt(n), with n - 1 degrees of freedom when conditions hold.

cards.front: Why use a t distribution for mean inference when population standard deviation is unknown?
cards.back: The sample standard deviation estimates sigma, adding uncertainty reflected by the t distribution's heavier tails.

cards.front: How does the t distribution change as degrees of freedom increase?
cards.back: It approaches the standard normal distribution.

cards.front: What is a null hypothesis?
cards.back: The baseline claim about a population parameter or model tested against an alternative.

cards.front: What is a p-value?
cards.back: Assuming the null hypothesis and model conditions, the probability of results at least as extreme as observed in the direction or directions specified by the alternative.

cards.front: What is the decision rule using significance level alpha?
cards.back: Reject the null hypothesis when the p-value is at most alpha; otherwise fail to reject it.

cards.front: Does failing to reject the null prove it true?
cards.back: No. The data may provide insufficient evidence against it.

cards.front: What is a Type I error?
cards.back: Rejecting a true null hypothesis.

cards.front: What is a Type II error?
cards.back: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis.

cards.front: What is the power of a statistical test?
cards.back: The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis for a specified alternative that is true; power equals 1 - beta.

cards.front: How does increasing sample size generally affect power, all else equal?
cards.back: It increases power by making real departures easier to detect.

cards.front: How does decreasing alpha generally affect power, all else equal?
cards.back: It decreases power while reducing the probability of a Type I error.

cards.front: What is the one-proportion z-test statistic?
cards.back: z = (p-hat - p0)/sqrt(p0(1 - p0)/n), when the null model and conditions apply.

cards.front: What is the one-sample t-test statistic?
cards.back: t = (x-bar - mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)), with n - 1 degrees of freedom under the standard conditions.

cards.front: How should paired quantitative data be analyzed for a mean comparison?
cards.back: Compute a difference for each pair and perform one-sample inference on the mean difference.

cards.front: What is the chi-square statistic for count data?
cards.back: Sum over categories or cells of (observed - expected) squared divided by expected.

cards.front: What does a chi-square goodness-of-fit test assess?
cards.back: Whether one categorical variable's observed counts are consistent with a specified distribution.

cards.front: What are the degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with k categories and no estimated parameters?
What is an expected cell count in a chi-square test of independence?
cards.back: Row total times column total divided by the grand total.

cards.front: What are the degrees of freedom for a chi-square test of independence in an r by c table?
What is a common expected-count condition for AP chi-square procedures?
cards.back: All expected counts are at least 5, along with suitable randomization and independence conditions.

cards.front: What null hypothesis does a regression slope t-test usually test?
cards.back: That the population linear-regression slope is zero, indicating no linear association in the modeled population.

cards.front: What are the degrees of freedom for a simple linear-regression slope t-test?
cards.back: n - 2, under the standard linear-model assumptions.
